text:
For years, Jenkins ran every merge we shipped, and it rarely complained. That didn't mean it was in good shape. Over time it had picked up a pile of plugins, hand-tuned agents and pipeline definitions, and only a few people on the team were comfortable editing any of it. Builds were slow, the bill went up every month, and just keeping the server alive took real ongoing work.

We moved our CI to GitHub Actions. It took three weeks to migrate all 41 pipelines, and we rewrote each one as a workflow stored in the same repo as the code it builds. It went better than we expected. Build time went from 14 minutes to 6, so developers hear back on their changes in less than half the time they used to. Our monthly CI bill dropped from $900 to $410, which comes to almost $6,000 a year.

Below we cover why we left Jenkins and how we did the migration without holding up development. We also get into the problems we hit along the way and what we'd change if we did it again.
